A B S T R A C T
Anaerobic co-digestion (AcoD) of sewage sludge (SS) with food waste (FW) is a practical approach in urban areas 
due to spatio-temporal availability of these co-substrates. While micro-aeration could enhance hydrolysis and 
control acidification during mono-digestion, the effects of micro-aeration on AcoD remains unclear. This study 
explored the influence of oxidation–reduction potential (ORP)-based in-situ micro-aeration on AcoD performance 
of SS and FW. Although mono-digestion of FW failed due to acidification and micro-aeration of SS was unstable 
due to high solids content and viscosity, micro-aeration improved specific biogas and methane yields by 21.1 % 
and 13.1 %, respectively, at the FW:SS ratio of 60:40 ((volatile solids (VS) basis). This improvement was observed 
at an organic loading rate of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d and alkalinity below 5000 mg CaCO3/L. The observed positive effect 
of micro-aeration was accompanied by changes in relative abundance of Aminicenantes. Functional analysis 
suggested that AcoD was driven by homoacetogenesis and acetoclastic methanogenesis.

1. Introduction
The rapid population growth and urbanization has further aggra­
vated issues with organic waste management, especially food waste 
(FW) and sewage sludge (SS). FW accounts for 62 % of household waste 
by mass, amounting to 77 kg per capita annually (UNEP, 2024). In 2022, 
total of 1.05 billion metric tons of FW were estimated to be generated 
from household, food service, and retailing (UNEP, 2024). Despite ef­
forts to address the issue, no significant improvement has been made 
in food loss, which remained at 13 % of the food produced (FAO, 2023). 
This amount of FW accounts for significant land and carbon footprints 
since food loss and waste generate an estimated 8–10 % of global 
greenhouse gases (GHGs) and take up nearly 30 % of agricultural land 
(UNEP, 2024). In the U.S. alone, food loss and waste management 
correspond to 170 million metric tons (MMT) of CO2e GHG emissions 
(excluding landfills). SS, a byproduct of activated sludge systems 
in wastewater treatment, is generated at a rate of 45 dry MMT per year 
(Gao et al., 2020). SS could contain organic compounds, trace elements, 
and organic nitrogen, though the concern is the potential presence of 
heavy metals. Among treatment methods like composting and inciner­
ation, anaerobic digestion (AD) stands out as the method with the lowest 
GHG emissions because it produces bioenergy (Piippo et al., 2018).
Anaerobic co-digestion (AcoD) has emerged as a promising and 
practical approach for managing organic wastes, offering improved 
system performance and stability due to the complementary character­
istics of different substrates, the enrichment of microbial consortia, 
improved quality of digestate, and reduced GHG emissions (Chuenchart 
et al., 2024). Recently, significant efforts have been made to improve 
biodegradability and enhance microbial synergy in AD process. One 
such approach, in-situ micro-aeration, involves introducing a small 
amount of oxygen into the aqueous phase of the digester at dosing rates 
of 0.01–5.00 mL-O2/L·d. However, detecting low oxygen levels in AD 
systems is challenging due to the limitations of DO probes (> 0.1 mg-O2/ 
L), which are not designed for high-solids environments (Yu et al., 
2020). As oxygen input increases, the system becomes more oxidative. 
Oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) serves as an indirect indicator of 
oxygen levels in AD systems and helps maintain an optimal range for 
effective micro-aeration (Nghiem et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2019).
Due to its high electronegativity, oxygen serves as a rapid electron 
acceptor within AD systems, facilitating organic matter degradation by 
facultative anaerobes, volatile fatty acids (VFAs) oxidation through 
β-oxidation, and sulfide removal via desulfurization (Nguyen et al., 
2019). Therefore, micro-aeration can either improve AD system per­
formance and stability or lead to acidification, depending on factors 
such as micro-aeration intensity, substrate composition, digester oper­
ational conditions, and microbial niches (Fu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). 
For example, in SS mono-digestion, micro-aeration at 12.5 mL-air/L⋅d 
improved specific biogas yield (SBY) and volatile solids (VS) reduction 
by 16 % and 18 %, respectively (Zhou et al., 2021). Similarly, in FW 
mono-digestion, micro-aeration within acidogenic reactor at 258 L-air/ 
kg total solids (TS)/d improved acetic acid production by 3-folds and 
enhanced soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD) production, as well 
as carbohydrate and protein degradation, by 21 %, 22 %, and 38 %, 
respectively. This resulted in 17 % improvement in specific methane 
yield (SMY) compared to non-micro-aerated condition. However, the 
same study reported that micro-aeration at intensities either higher or 
lower than 258 L-air/kg TS/d resulted in a 17–26 % reduction in SMY 
(Xu et al., 2014).
Despite the growing interest in the application of micro-aeration 
technology in AD field, studies on its effects in AcoD systems remain 
limited. For example, micro-aeration pretreatment (4 days, 37.5 mL-O2/ 
LR⋅d) improved sCOD of hydrolysate by 13 %, leading to 23 % increase 
in SMY compared to non-micro-aerated condition in AcoD of FW and 
brown water (150 g: 2 L) (Lim and Wang, 2013). In a sequencing batch 
system, in-situ micro-aeration (375 mL-air/L⋅d) improved SMY by 22 %, 
as well as effluent sCOD by 67 % and VFAs by 58 %, in the AcoD of 
poultry litter and wheat straw (1:1, mass basis) compared to non-micro- 
aerated condition (Zhan et al., 2023). In contrast, in-situ micro-aeration 
(1000 mL-air/L⋅d) during AcoD of swine manure with corn silage 
(17.1:111.2, mass basis) resulted in higher acidification, increasing 
VFAs and lactic acid concentrations by 20 % and 19 %, respectively, 
compared to non-micro-aerated condition (Cao et al., 2022). Given these 
mixed and inconclusive effects, micro-aeration may help stabilize AcoD 
system for FW and SS co-digestion by regulating VFA accumulation 
across different co-substrate ratios. Furthermore, no long-term studies 
have explored the effects of in-situ micro-aeration on AcoD system 
performance and microbial community dynamics.
This study evaluated the effect of ORP-based in-situ micro-aeration 
on the performance and stability of an AcoD system, compared to non- 
micro-aerated (anaerobic) conditions, using varying co-substrate ratios 
and organic loading rates (OLRs). Initially, the FW to SS ratio (FW:SS, VS 
basis) was optimized, with the highest SMY observed at FW:SS ratio of 
80:20. Subsequently, the OLR was gradually increased from 2.25 to 4.0 
and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d in a stepwise approach. Additionally, microbial com­
munity dynamics were monitored throughout the long-term semi- 
continuous operation of the AcoD system.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Post-consumer FW, which was a mixture of cooked food, fruit peel, 
and vegetable scraps, was collected for a week in the spring of 2020 from 
Gateway Caf´e at University of Hawai’i at M¯anoa. The FW mixture was 
blended using a mechanical blender (Vitamix VM0185A, USA), sieved 
through a 5-mm pore size sieve, and thoroughly mixed to ensure ho­
mogenization. SS, which was a mixture of primary solids and waste 
activated sludge retrieved from the belt filter press, and anaerobically 
digested waste activated sludge (ADWAS) were obtained in the spring of 
2020 from Hawai’i Kai wastewater treatment plant, Honolulu, HI, USA. 
Both FW and SS were stored at −20 ◦C, while the (ADWAS) was stored at 
4 ◦C until further use. The characteristics of FW, SS, and ADWAS used in 
this study are summarized in Karki et al. (2022). ADWAS was used as an 
inoculum at the initial stage of digester operation. After the system was 
started, the digestate from each stage of digester operation was collected 
and stored in an air-tight container at 25 ◦C.
2.2. Semi-continuous system operation and in-situ micro-aeration
AD study was conducted using two, 8-L continuous stirred-tank re­
actors (CSTRs) with working volume of 6 L and mixing speed of 120 
rpm, and operated in semi-continuous mode under mesophilic condition 
(35 ± 1 ◦C) at a hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 20 days. Each reactor 
was installed with an ORP control system (pH/ORP 400, Cole-Parmer, 
USA) as previously described in Nguyen et al. (2019) and a perforated 
aeration tube for ORP-based in-situ micro-aeration. The mono-digestion 
of SS and FW was evaluated in parallel, starting at an OLR of 1.00 g VS/ 
L⋅d. The FW mono-digestion failed even at an OLR of 1.00 g VS/L⋅d due 
to acidification (pH = 6.80 and total volatile fatty acid-to-total alkalinity 
(VFA/ALK) ratio = 0.530 g HAc (acetic acid equivalent)/g CaCO3) and 
was discontinued. The SS mono-digestion was tested at an OLR up to 
2.25 g VS/L⋅d —the maximum possible at an HRT of 20 days due to 
intrinsic characteristics of SS. AcoD of FW and SS was initiated at the 
FW:SS ratio of 40:60 (VS basis) at an OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d. ORP-based 
in-situ micro-aeration was initially tested at +10 mV above the baseline 
ORP of −569 mV. A significant amount of injected oxygen escaped into 
the headspace. To address this issue and enhance oxygen mass transfer, 
biogas was recirculated through the bottom of the reactor. Then the 
effect of intermittent (every alternate day) in-situ micro-aeration at an 
ORP of +25 mV above the baseline ORP (under anaerobic conditions) 
was evaluated at an OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d across different co-substrate 
mixing ratios, with increasing content of FW in the mixture (i.e., FW:

on AcoD of FW and SS was further studied at OLRs of 4.0 and 6.0 g VS/

The average oxygen injection varied from 29 to 82 mL-O2/L⋅d, 
depending on the intrinsic oxygen needed to achieve the targeted ORP. 
Each stage was maintained for at least 20 days in a quasi-steady state, 
defined by no significant difference (p > 0.05) in SMY for five consec­
utive days of operation (see supplementary materials). Part of the data 
from non-microaerated condition was used for machine learning model 
verification in our previous study (Chuenchart et al., 2024).
2.3. Analytical methods
Biogas production and composition, pH, VFA/ALK ratio, and indi­
vidual VFAs were analyzed periodically. The volume of the biogas was 
measured using a drum-type gas counter (TG 0.5/5 drum-type gas 
meter, Ritter, Germany) and normalized to standard temperature (273 
K) and pressure (1 atm). The composition of biogas was determined 
using a gas chromatograph equipped with a thermal conductivity de­
tector (GC-TCD) (490 Micro GC System, Agilent, USA). pH, alkalinity 
(ALK), total VFA, and VFA/ALK ratio were measured using an auto- 
titrator (TitraLab AT1000, Hach, USA) with a pH probe (PHC805). TS 
and VS were determined following the Standard Methods (APHA, 2017). 
Individual VFA concentrations were determined using a gas chromato­
graph with a flame ionization detector (GC-FID) (GC-2014, Shimadzu, 
Japan). sCOD and total ammonia nitrogen were determined using HACH 
TNT 823 and TNT 834, respectively.
2.4. Microbial community analysis
Biomass samples were collected from the digesters across all exper­
imental conditions and were stored at −20 ◦C until further processed. 
DNA extractions were performed in triplicates using the Maxwell 16 RSC 
Blood DNA kit (Promega, USA), according to modified manufacturer’s 
instructions. Briefly, the samples were initially mixed with 0.5 g zirco­
nium beads and 600 uL lysis buffer. Three cycles of 2 min bead beating 
using the Mini-BeadBeater-24 (BioSpec Products, USA) and centrifuga­
tion at 12,500×g for 10 min were performed to collect the supernatant, 
after which proteinase K was added. After incubation at 56 ◦C for 20 
min, DNA extracts were obtained following automated extraction using 
the Maxwell® RSC 48 Instrument (Promega, USA). DNA concentrations 
and quality were determined using NanoDrop One Spectrophotometer 
(Thermo Fisher, USA). Microbial sequencing was performed at the 
University of Michigan’s Microbiome Core facility (University of Mich­
igan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA), targeting the V4 region of the 16S rRNA 
gene, using modified earth microbiome project (EMP) primers (Kozich 
et al., 2013). Multiplexed amplicons were sequenced using Illumina 
MiSeq using the MiSeq reagent kit V2 (2 × 250 bp reads) according to 
the manufacturer’s instructions with modifications found in the EMP 
SOP (Caporaso et al., 2012; Parada et al., 2016). FASTQ files were 
generated for paired-end reads and were analyzed using the Schloss 
MiSeq SOP on the Mothur bioinformatics platform. Sequences were 
filtered, and chimeras were removed using the UCHIME algorithm, after 
which the sequences were aligned using the SILVA reference database 
(Quast et al., 2013). Further analysis was carried out using operational 
taxonomic unit (OTU) clustering based on an average neighbor algo­
rithm at a 3 % cutoff limit. The software package Tax4Fun2 was used in 
the R environment to predict functional capabilities using the taxonomic 
profile to predict the metabolic pathways in the Kyoto Encyclopedia of 
Genes and Genomes (KEGG). OTUs were mapped to reference se­
quences, and the taxonomic abundance was converted into the relative 
abundance of enzyme-encoding genes associated with KEGG pathways 
and orthologs. All raw sequences are available in the National Center for 
Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under 
BioProject ID: PRJNA1217127.
2.5. Statistical analysis
The effect of co-substrate mixing ratios, OLRs, and micro-aeration on 
SBY, SMY, VS reduction, pH, ALK, VFA, and VFA/ALK ratio were 
analyzed using t-test with a significance level of p < 0.05. Violin plot and 
statistical analysis were conducted using the following packages: car, 
ggplot2, Imer4, meta and ImerTest in Rstudio (R studio v.1.2.5033, 
USA). For the microbial community analysis, the redundancy analysis 
(RDA) was applied, the α-diversity and β-diversity were analyzed, and 
statistical significance was calculated following two-tailed unpaired 
Student’s t-test, analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA), and homo­
geneity of molecular variance (HOMOVA) with statistical significance at 
p < 0.05. Summary statistical analyses were conducted in exploratory 
and comparative manners, including Pearson correlation analysis, RDA, 
and Hedges’ g standardized mean differences (SMD, Eq. (1) with 
a random effect model. To account for the effects of micro-aeration, a 
standardized performance index (SPI) was used. The SPI was calculated 
as the average of standardized mean differences (effect sizes) of per­
formance parameters (x) including SMY, SBY, and VS reduction (Eq. (2).

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effects of co-substrate ratio and micro-aeration on system 
performance and stability
3.1.1. Start-up phases
At the beginning of SS mono-digestion (OLR = 1.00 g VS/L⋅d), SMY 
reached 210 NmL/g VS within the first week (Fig. 1a) with the VFA/ALK 
ratio of 0.198 g HAc/g CaCO3 and pH of 7.17. During this stage (i.e., SS 
mono-digestion at an OLR of 1.00 g VS/L⋅d), SMY varied between 170 
and 302 NmL/g VS with the VFA/ALK ratio of 0.207 ± 0.057 g HAc/g 
CaCO3 (pH = 7.27 ± 0.09). Subsequently, OLR was increased to 2.25 g 
VS/L⋅d (Stage I) (Fig. 1a). At this stage, SBY and SMY were 260 ± 29 and 
190 ± 19 NmL/g VS, respectively, with VS reduction of 38.8 ± 2.3 % 
(Fig. 1b, c, d). pH remained within an acceptable range at 7.78 ± 0.05 
with the VFA/ALK ratio of 0.299 ± 0.040 g HAc/g CaCO3 (Fig. 1e, f), 
indicating stable digester performance. However, micro-aeration (+25 
mV) during the mono-digestion of SS at an OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d (days 
178–188) led to digester instability, resulting in near failure with SMY 
dropping to 89 NmL/g VS. This instability may have been caused by the 
high viscosity of the digester contents (TS > 4.0 %), which hindered 
oxygen mass transfer. A significant portion of the injected oxygen 
escaped to the headspace, resulting in 10 % oxygen content (v/v) in the 
biogas.
To address the high viscosity issue of the digester contents, AcoD 
with FW was initiated at the SS:FW ratio of 40:60 (VS basis) while 
maintaining the same OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d (Stage II). During this stage, 
SBY and SMY increased to 401 ± 22 and 278 ± 22 NmL/g VS, respec­
tively, with an improved VS reduction of 47.8 ± 3.5 %. The pH dropped 
to 7.57 ± 0.14 with the VFA/ALK ratio of 0.309 ± 0.046 g HAc/g 
CaCO3, indicating increased acidification due to the high biodegrad­
ability of FW. However, a steady balance between acidification and 
buffering was maintained (Fig. 1b-d). Compared to SS mono-digestion, 
AcoD significantly improved SBY, SMY, and VS reduction by 54.2 %, 
46.3 %, and 23.2 %, respectively. Meanwhile, the digester fed with FW

3.1.2. Effects of co-substrate ratio on system performance and stability
After successfully developing micro-aeration coupled with biogas 
recirculation, AcoD at the FW:SS ratio of 40:60 was evaluated under 
biogas recirculation (Stage III). Compared to without biogas recircula­
tion, biogas recirculation significantly improved SBY, SMY, and VS 
reduction by 13.5 %, 10.8 %, and 11.9 %, respectively, yielding 
respective values of 455 ± 94 NmL/g VS, 308 ± 65 NmL/g VS, and 53.5 
± 1.4 %. Additionally, pH and the VFA/ALK ratio remained within the 
acceptable range at 7.45 ± 0.06 and 0.314 ± 0.188 g HAc/g CaCO3, 
respectively. The significant improvement in performance after biogas 
recirculation was likely due to better mass transfer and solid–liquid 
interface exchange, as well as a shift in the microbial community (Zhao 
et al., 2020).

In contrast, consistent increases in SBY and SMY were observed 
under micro-aerobic conditions (Stages IV, VI, and VIII). Compared to 
the FW:SS ratio of 40:60, ratios of 60:40 and 80:20 improved SBY by 
23.6 % and 32.2 %, resulting in 556 ± 59 and 595 ± 37 NmL/g VS, 
respectively. The corresponding SMY values also improved by 12.7 % 
and 23.2 %, reaching 345 ± 39 and 377 ± 19 NmL/g VS, respectively. 
Additionally, VS reduction increased from 53.8 ± 0.6 % to 60.3 ± 1.2 % 
and 62.3 ± 0.6 %, representing 12.1 % and 15.8 % increases, respec­

carbon content than SS (see supplementary materials), likely contrib­
uted to the efficient conversion of VS in FW into biogas.
Overall, the higher FW content in co-substrate mixture led to 
increased SBY, SMY, and VS reduction, as evidenced by strong positive 
correlations (R > 0.70) (Fig. 1.g). Additionally, negative correlations 
between FW content and pH, ALK and VFA indicated rapid conversion of 
organic matter to VFA and biogas at higher FW levels in the co-substrate 
mixture.
3.1.3. Effects of micro-aeration on system performance and stability
The effects of micro-aeration on system performance varied with 
different FW and SS mixing ratios (Stage III-VIII), influenced by their 
aggregate characteristics on VFA production and consumption. During 
the initial phase (FW:SS ratio of 40:60, Stage IV), micro-aeration did not 
significantly impact the AcoD performance and stability parameters 
(SBY, SMY, VS reduction, and pH). The significant decrease in the VFA/ 
ALK ratio from 0.556 to 0.150 g HAc/g CaCO3 was due to the adaptation 
to biogas recirculation (Fig. 1f). At FW:SS ratio of 60:40, micro-aeration 
significantly improved SBY by 21.1 % (556 ± 59 NmL/g VS) and SMY by 
13.1 % (345 ± 39 NmL/g VS) compared to anaerobic conditions (459 ±
43 and 305 ± 31 NmL/g VS, respectively). This performance improve­
ment, despite no change in VS reduction, was likely due to the 35 % 
higher organic carbon content in FW than SS, leading to increased 
biogas production per unit of VS consumed. Additionally, micro- 
aeration had a pronounced effect on stability parameters, improving 
pH from 7.39 ± 0.05 to 7.43 ± 0.05 and the VFA/ALK ratio from 0.207 
± 0.033 to 0.254 ± 0.033 g HAc/g CaCO3. At the FW:SS ratio of 80:20, 
only SBY increased by 7.8 % (from 552 ± 50 to 595 ± 37 NmL/g VS), 
while SMY, VS reduction, pH, and the VFA/ALK ratio remained nearly 
unchanged compared to anaerobic conditions.
Overall, higher FW content (i.e., FW:SS ratios of 60:40 and 80:20) 
enhanced SBY (CH4, CO2, and H2) due to enhanced anaerobic fermen­
tation of readily hydrolyzable and/or soluble organic matter within FW. 
The enhanced facultative activity under micro-aerobic condition likely 
have contributed to the increased CO2 production. Consequently, 
increased availability of CO2 can improve hydrogenotrophic methano­
genesis, depending on the availability of hydrogen and substrate types 
(Nguyen et al., 2019). Despite variations in FW:SS ratios (from 40:60 to 
80:20), pH and the VFA/ALK ratio remained fairly stable within the 
ranges of 7.20–7.60 and 0.180–0.320 g HAc/g CaCO3, respectively, 
indicating a stable AD system. Furthermore, the concentrations of in­
dividual VFAs remained fairly low, with acetic acid below 400 mg/L and 
all other VFAs below 100 mg/L. The effects of micro-aeration were 
inconsistent across different co-substrate ratios, likely due to the low 
OLR. Therefore, further experiments were conducted to investigate its 
impact on digester stability at higher OLRs.
3.2. Effects of organic loading rate and micro-aeration on system 
performance and stability
3.2.1. Effects of organic loading rate on system performance and stability
The FW:SS ratio of 80:20, which yielded the highest SBY and SMY at 
an OLR of 2.25 VS/L⋅d, was selected to investigate the effect of micro- 
aeration on digester stability at higher OLRs of 4.0 and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d. 
To improve the reproducibility, second and third trials were conducted 
in a parallel-operated second digester (Fig. 2a). Overall, the results were 
highly consistent across the trials, except during the failure stage at an 
OLR of 6.0 g VS/L⋅d, where data were excluded from analysis.
Under anaerobic conditions, at OLRs of 2.25, 4.0, and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d, 
SBY values were 578 ± 46, 669 ± 29, and 693 ± 32 NmL/g VS, 
respectively, with corresponding SMY values of 385 ± 35, 434 ± 31, 
470 ± 29 NmL/g VS. Increases in OLRs from 2.25 to 4.0 and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d 
corresponded to improvement in SBY by 15.7 % and 19.7 %, and SMY by 
12.7 % and 22.0 %, respectively. VS reduction showed a similar trend, 
reaching 64.2 ± 1.9 %, 66.7 ± 2.0 %, and 65.8 ± 1.0 % at OLRs of 2.25, 
4.0 and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d, respectively, representing increases of 3.8 % and 
2.5 % compared to the lowest OLR tested. The improvements in per­
formance parameters (SBY, SMY, and VS reduction) at an OLR of 4.0 g 
VS/L⋅d, followed by decreases or insignificant changes at an OLR of 6.0 g 
VS/L⋅d suggest potential system inhibition at the highest OLR tested 
(Fig. 2 a-c).
Under micro-aerobic conditions, increasing OLR from 2.25 to 4.0 g 
VS/L⋅d resulted in an increase in SBY from 626 ± 44 to 669 ± 76 NmL/g 
VS and SMY from 403 ± 33 to 430 ± 53 NmL/g VS, reflecting im­
provements of 6.9 % and 6.7 %, respectively. Although the pH increased 
from 7.26 ± 0.03 to 7.41 ± 0.15, the VFA/ALK ratio also increased 
from 0.243 ± 0.048 to 0.387 ± 0.175 g HAc/g CaCO3. Additionally, 
total VFA concentration significantly increased from 1.9 to 10.2 mmol/L 
(5.4-fold increase), indicating initial VFA accumulation during micro- 
aeration (Fig. 2k). However, at an OLR of 6.0 g VS/L⋅d, SBY and SMY 
decreased to 646 ± 75 and 419 ± 53 NmL/g VS, respectively, prior to 
system failure due to excessive VFA accumulation (Fig. 2d).
As OLR increased, VFA, ALK, total ammonia, and sCOD concentra­
tions consistently and significantly increased in both conditions, as 
indicated by moderate to strong correlations (Fig. 2f-g, i-j, and l). This is 
likely due to a high ammonia and organic nitrogen content in both FW 
and SS, as reflected by the low C/N ratio of 11.9 at the FW:SS ratio of 
80:20. Total ammonia levels increased to 1500 ± 120 and 2560 ± 160 
mg N/L but remained below the inhibition threshold for AD (i.e., 4000 
mg N/L) (Yan et al., 2020). However, this increase in total ammonia 
could partially inhibit acetoclastic methanogenesis, with an IC50 of 2130 
mg N/L (Wang et al., 2022). The system failure at an OLR of 6.0 g VS/L⋅d 
suggests that the optimal OLR for FW and SS ACoD at the FW:SS ratio of 
80:20 (VS basis) falls below 6.0 g VS/L⋅d for both micro-aerobic and 
anaerobic conditions.
3.2.2. Effects of micro-aeration on system performance and stability
The effects of micro-aeration on SBY and SMY varied across OLRs, 
demonstrating enhancement, neutrality, or reduction (Fig. 2b, c, and 
m). This was reflected in the SMD (negative, zero, and positive) and SPI 
values of 0.483, −0.213, and −0.493 for OLRs of 2.25, 4.0 and 6.0 g VS/ 
L⋅d, respectively (Fig. 2m). At an OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d, micro-aeration 
significantly improved SBY and SMY by 8.3 % (from 578 ± 46 to 626 ±
44 NmL/g VS) and 4.4 % (from 385 ± 35 to 403 ± 33 NmL/g VS), 
respectively. Additionally, pH and the VFA/ALK ratio remained fairly 
stable at 7.25 ± 0.03 and 0.228 ± 0.030 g HAc/g CaCO3, respectively. 
However, at an OLR of 4.0 g VS/L⋅d, micro-aeration had no significant 
effect on either SBY or SMY. During micro-aeration, VS reduction, pH, 
ALK remained unchanged at 65.7 ± 1.6 %, 7.41 ± 0.15, and 5619 ± 551 
mg CaCO3/L, respectively. However, increases in VFA from 1434 ± 179 
to 2109 ± 742 mg HAc/L and the VFA/ALK ratio from 0.244 ± 0.028 to 
0.389 ± 0.175 g HAc/g CaCO3 indicated the beginning of VFA accu­
mulation during micro-aeration.

cated inhibition due to VFA accumulation during micro-aeration. Acetic 
acid concentrations increased significantly, reaching 4690–4860 mg 
HAc/L (78.1–80.8 mmol/L), while propionic acid levels increased to 
426–549 mg HPro/L (5.8–7.8 mmol/L) (Fig. 2k). Furthermore, titrated 
total VFAs (~10,000 mg HAc/L) exceeded the sum of identified indi­
vidual VFAs (~5500 mg HAc/L), suggesting the accumulation of other 
organic acids, such as medium- and long-chain fatty acids. The increase 
in sCOD from 6700 to 10,400 mg COD/L after micro-aeration further 
indicated the potential accumulation of soluble organic compounds. 
However, micro-aeration did not affect ammonia concentration.
SMD and SPI also indicated that micro-aeration led to lower pH and 
ALK, along with higher VFA levels and VFA/ALK ratios, suggesting VFA 
accumulation and inhibition of methanogenesis (Fig. 2m). At an OLR of 
4.0 g VS/L⋅d, increased hydrolysis and acetogenesis were observed, as 
indicated by higher total VFA and higher individual VFA levels (Fig. 2d, 
f, and k). Therefore, no significant differences in SBY and SMY were 
observed between the micro-aerobic and control conditions at this OLR, 
while system inhibition occurred at an OLR of 6.0 g VS/L⋅d.
Despite the previous study reporting the effectiveness of micro- 
aeration in overcoming VFA accumulation during the AD of lignocel­
lulosic feedstock, such as Napier grass (Pennisetum purpureum) at an OLR 
of 5.0 g VS/L⋅d (Nguyen et al., 2019), this study observed inconsistent 
effects of micro-aeration on AcoD. This inconsistency can be attributed 
to the highly alkaline nature of SS, the readily hydrolyzable character­
istics of FW, and the inherent competition between homoacetogens and 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens, which is influenced by the nature of co- 
substrates. When ALK is below 5,000 mg CaCO3/L, micro-aeration can 
effectively control accumulated VFAs by enhancing VFA oxidation. 
However, when ALK exceeds this threshold, micro-aeration may dete­
riorate digester performance due to increased VFA accumulation. 
Additionally, during the AD of readily hydrolyzable substrates at high 
OLRs, micro-aeration may exacerbate VFA accumulation as facultative 
bacteria ferment more organic matter to organic acids, disrupting the 
VFA-ALK balance.
In systems where hydrolysis is the rate-limiting step—such as those 
digesting lignocellulosic biomass and animal manure (e.g., corn straw 
(Fu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2022), Napier grass (Nguyen et al., 2019), 
poultry litter and wheat straw (Zhan et al., 2023))—micro-aeration has 
been shown to improve AD performance by promoting the activity of 
hydrolytic bacteria (Fu et al., 2023). In contrast, during the AD of readily 
hydrolyzable substrates, such as FW (Xu et al., 2014) and wastewater 
(Salom´e Duarte et al., 2024), micro-aeration can lead to the accumula­
tion of sCOD and organic acids, especially at high OLRs.
3.3. Microbial community dynamics
3.3.1. Bacterial communities
Amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene revealed that varied co- 
digestion and OLR periods greatly shifted community structure, espe­
cially with respect to the initial mono-digestion phase. A non-metric 
multidimensional scaling (NMDS) plot based on Bray-Curtis distance 
matrix indicated that the divergence of the microbial community from 
mono-digestion to FW:SS mixing ratios resulted in higher partitioning of 
microbial groups along NMDS 2 axis, suggesting an influence of the 
feeding regime on community structure (AMOVA, p-value < 0.05). 
Although it was apparent that the communities at an OLR of 6.0 g VS/L⋅d 
were relatively similar, the shift along both NMDS 1 and NMDS 2 axes 
was significant compared to the rest of the samples, in addition to the 
separation of the microbial groups at lower OLRs (HOMOVA, p-value <
0.05) (see supplementary materials).
A calculation of diversity metrics included the Shannon Index (H’), 
richness (S), and invSimpson (1/D). Results showed an initial increase in 
S during co-digestion and at different FW:SS ratios, but a general 
decreasing trend in diversity was observed across biomass samples at 
increasing OLRs (see supplementary materials). The mono-digestion 
period, indeed, had the highest overall diversity and eventually 
decreased from 3.51 to 2.02 for H’ and from 223 to 145 for S. Evaluating 
the relative abundance (RA) of populations throughout the experiment 
revealed a prominent shift in the three most abundant phyla, Chloro­
flexi, Bacteroidetes, and Firmicutes, known to be either strict or facul­
tative anaerobic fermentative groups. The mono-digestion period was 
dominated by Firmicutes (with RA 46.0 %), while Chloroflexi thrived at 
increased FW:SS ratios at an OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d, with RA ranges be­
tween 40–50 %, after which Bacteroidetes were observed to dominate 
when OLR was increased to 4.0 g VS/L⋅d and then to 6.0 g VS/L⋅d, 
reaching a maximum of 68.7 % (Fig. 3a). It is also noteworthy to 
mention that Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes abundances were relatively 
stable during the increased FW:SS ratios. These groups were previously 
found to correlate with VFA production, namely acetic and propionic 
acids, during the long-term mesophilic AD of FW and SS at increasing 
mixing ratios (Owusu-Agyeman et al., 2023). A closer look at the genus- 
level RA distribution revealed top genera that likely contributed to the 
shift in microbial communities (Fig. 3b). Genera that contributed to 
significant changes during the co-substrate variation period were un­
classified Ruminococcaceae (homo-acetogens), unclassified Syntropho­
monadaceae (anaerobic syntrophs), and unclassified Actinomycetaceae 
(facultatively anaerobic bacteria), with increasing RAs in general, and 
unclassified Pseudomonadaceae with decreasing overall RAs (t-test, p- 
value < 0.05). Based on these observations, it is apparent that the mi­
crobial groups varied greatly during the co-substrate variation period, 
mainly because of adaptation to the complex substrate being introduced 
throughout the increasing FW:SS ratios and micro-aeration application. 
On the other hand, the genera that contributed to significant changes 
during the OLR variation period were unclassified Bacteroidetes 
(increased RAs in general), Syntrophomonas, unclassified Bacteroidales, 
Bacteroides, unclassified Syntrophaceae, and unclassified Meth­
anobacteriaceae, with decreasing RAs in general (t-test, p-value < 0.05). 
Genera that significantly changed during both periods were related to 
unclassified Clostridiales spp., unclassified Anaerolineaceae spp., unclas­
sified Dysgonomonadaceae spp., Aminipila, unclassified Prolixibacteraceae 
spp., Sedimentibacter, Proteiniborus, and Romboutsia. For example, un­
classified Anaerolineaceae significantly increased from 12.6 % to 47.3 % 
initially and decreased to 3.30 % at the end of the experiment, while 
Aminipila decreased overall (from 2.14 % to 0.06 %), while Sed­
imentibacter initially decreased from 0.72 % to 0.06 % and then 
increased again to 0.10 %, respectively (t-test, p-value < 0.05). These 
genera are either strict anaerobes or facultative anaerobes, which in­
dicates that the impact of micro-aeration on community structure should 
not be overlooked even at low RA. It is likely that micro-aeration

3.3.2. Archaeal communities
Archaeal community structure changed considerably during co- 
digestion and OLR variation periods compared to the mono-digestion 
phase. The archaeal community was dominated by three main fam­
ilies: Methanobacteriaceae spp. initially during the mono-digestion 
phase, Methanotrichaceae spp. starting co-digestion with consistent 
high abundances, and Methanospirillaceae spp. at higher OLRs, with 
gradually increased abundances at OLR of 4.0 g VS/L⋅d and OLR of 6.0 g 
VS/L⋅d, respectively, which were aligned with the increased SBY and 
SMY during these phases (Fig. 4a). Among the genera classified, Meth­
anobacterium spp., Methanobrevibacter spp., Methanoculleus spp., Meth­
anolinea spp., Methanomethylovorans spp., and Methanosarcina spp. were 
only observed during the co-digestion period at an OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d, 
after which a higher selectivity occurred at OLRs of 4.0 and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d. 
More specifically, three genera related to Methanothrix spp. (Methano­
thrix soehngenii sequence identified at 99.2 %), Methanospirillum spp. 
(Methanospirillum hungatei sequence identified at 95.3 %), and Meth­
anomassiliicoccus spp. contributed to more than 90 % of the archaeal 
community at the end of the experiment, with the latter two having 
slightly increased RAs (Fig. 4b). These observations indicated that 
although methanogens were resilient to the different conditions, given 
that CH4 production was not affected initially, an OLR of 6.0 g VS/L⋅d 
likely served as a threshold for these selective methanogens to survive. 
Predictive functionality capabilities of the microbial community were 
further studied using Tax4FUN2 and KEGG. Key modules and corre­
sponding unique orthologs that relate to the methanogenesis were 
selected to identify predicted genes encoding for key enzymes (see 
supplementary

(M00357), hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (M00567), and the 
reductive acetyl-CoA pathway (M00377) for homo-acetogens (Rama 
et al., 2024). Upon starting co-digestion, hydrogenotrophic methano­
genesis and homoacetogenesis capabilities increased (a shift from ace­
toclastic methanogenesis), which partially explains the positive effect on 
the system’s performance. Interestingly, all three were observed to have 
decreased capabilities at the end of the experiment (Fig. 5a). Further, 
hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis increased when biogas recirculation 
was introduced, which aligns with the positive effects reported on sys­
tem’s stability, likely due to the readily available CO2. In addition, the 
decrease in acetoclastic pathway and Methanothrix spp. at an OLR of 6.0 
g VS/L⋅d was likely linked to the decreased SMY observed. Meth­
anospirillum spp. and Methanothrix spp. are both capable of using CO2 or 
acetate to produce CH4, while Methanomassiliicoccus spp. can use 
methylamine/dimethylamine/trimethylamine to produce CH4. On the 
other hand, the dominance of Methanospirillum spp. is explained by their 
ability to survive under oxygenated environments due to their antioxi­
dant features (Lyu and Lu, 2018). Species related to Methanospirillum, 
namely M. hungatei, can produce CH4 by utilizing H2 and formate as 
electron donors to reduce CO2 in syntrophy with Syntrophomonas. 
Coincidentally, Syntrophomonas genera identified in our study signifi­
cantly increased during the highest OLR tested (i.e., 6.0 g VS/L⋅d) (t-test, 
p-value < 0.05) with two species identified: Syntrophomonas bryantii (at 
confidence level 97.2 %) and Syntrophomonas wolfei (at confidence level 
94.9 %). These two species are phylogenetically closely related and have 
been studied for cooperation via butyrate oxidation (Crable et al., 2016; 
Walker et al., 2019). In addition, microbial communities related to 
homoacetogenesis and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathways 
have been reported to compete for H2, and the higher capabilities of key 
enzymes with the homoacetogenesis pathway likely relate to the acetate 
accumulation observed during the highest OLR, especially that unclas­
sified Ruminococcaceae, among key homoacetogens, were also abundant 
(Karekar et al., 2022). Homoacetogens have higher adaptability to 
acidic and alkaline conditions, at which they outcompete hydro­
genotrophs as well (Mosbæk et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2021). Further, an 
alternative acetate-degrading community involves a synergy between 
syntrophic acetate oxidizers (SAOB), slow growers, and hydro­
genotrophic methanogens. A few syntrophic acetate oxidizing genera 
were merely present in the microbiome consortia, with decreased RAs at 
< 1 % (see supplementary materials), indicating that this pathway did 
not likely prevail under the reported conditions. Overall, methanogens 
were resilient to increased FW:SS ratios and micro-aeration, while 
diverse pathways were maintained at an OLR of 4.0 g VS/L⋅d.
3.3.3. Effects of operational parameters on microbial communities
The potential relationship between the experimental parameters and 
the abundance of microbial communities was further studied using the 
RDA and the significance was tested using ANOVA (Fig. 5b). Only the 
most abundant phyla were plotted to avoid cluttering. The experimental 
parameters chosen included the different OLRs, FW:SS ratios, and SPI. 
OLR and FW:SS ratio constraints significantly affected the microbial 
composition (ANOVA, p-value < 0.05). In addition, the two RDA com­
ponents were found to explain 82.3 % of data variability, and that 
illustrated the associations between the variables and experimental 
conditions. The length of the arrow indicates the extent to which the 
selected environmental variables explain the taxonomy, while arrows in 
opposite directions show a negative correlation. The results showed a 
strong positive correlation between OLR and Bacteroidetes and a weaker 
correlation with OLR and Spirochaetes. SPI, however, showed the 
highest positive correlation with Aminicenantes, an organotroph with 
carbohydrates and proteinaceous fermentation metabolism (Kadnikov 
et al., 2019), and a weaker correlation with Actinobacteria. Further, 
Chloroflexi correlated the most with FW:SS ratio of 60:40, as similarly 
indicated above.
Nevertheless, micro-aeration did not seem to alter microorganisms 
while additional CO2 was supplied and was not responsible for the 
system failure. Despite no strong evidence in the current results to 
explain sCOD accumulation and hydrolysis inhibition, further investi­
gation of microbial activities needs to be conducted to understand the 
prevailing mechanisms.
4. Proposed mechanisms
The positive effects of micro-aeration on system performance and 
stability were observed when ALK was lower than 5000 mg CaCO3/L, 
under conditions where OLR was 2.25 g VS/L⋅d, and FW:SS ratios were 
60:40 (trial 1) and 80:20 (trials 1–3). However, these positive effects 
became insignificant when ALK exceeded 5000 mg CaCO3/L under 
conditions, including 1) OLR of 2.25 g VS/L⋅d with the FW:SS ratio of 
40:60 and 2) OLRs of 4.0 and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d with the FW:SS ratio of 80:20. 
At lower ALK, VFAs can be converted to CO2 during micro-aeration, 
which can then be utilized by homoacetogens to produce acetate, 
which is subsequently converted into CH4 via acetoclastic methano­
genesis (Fig. 5c). Under these conditions, hydrolysis becomes a rate- 
limiting step due to the low concentrations of metabolic intermediates 
(e.g., acetate and CO2). Therefore, micro-aeration enhances hydrolysis 
and acidogenesis by promoting the growth and activity of diverse 
facultative anaerobes.
In contrast, when ALK is higher than 5000 mg CaCO3/L, owing to 
high OLRs and conversion of substrates, including complex biopolymers,

not improve system performance under OLRs of 4.0 and 6.0 g VS/L⋅d, 
with ALK exceeding 5000 mg CaCO3/L. Moreover, at high OLRs, where 
methanogenesis was inhibited due to system acidification (Acetic acid =

pathways.
Several studies have reported that micro-aeration enhances perfor­
mance of AD under low ALK conditions, such as during the digestion of 
Napier grass (ALK = 2880–3590 mg CaCO3/L) (Nguyen et al., 2019), 
poultry litter and wheat straw (ALK = 1240–1550 mg CaCO3/L) (Zhan 
et al., 2023), swine wastewater (ALK = 590–640 mg CaCO3/L) 
(Guimar˜aes de Oliveira et al., 2021), and SS (ALK = 1065 mg CaCO3/L) 
(Morello et al., 2021). Conversely, due to the presence of homoaceto­
genic anaerobes, micro-aeration led to acid accumulation during AD of 
organic fraction of municipal solid waste under high ALK conditions 
(ALK = 15480–18000 mg CaCO3/L) (Bacab et al., 2020). While this 
trend is consistent across different substrates, the improvement in hy­
drolysis and low ALK of the (co-)substrates likely played a significant 
role in AD system performance and stability. Additionally, the potential 
contribution of micro-aeration to VFAs and medium- to long-chain fatty 
acids production should not be overlooked (Duarte et al., 2018; Fu et al., 
2023; Xu et al., 2014).
5. Conclusions
Micro-aeration contributed to the AcoD system performance pri­
marily through improved hydrolysis. Performance improvements were 
observed only in FW:SS ratios of 60:40 and 80:20 at an OLR of 2.25 g VS/ 
L⋅d, when ALK was below 5000 mg CaCO3/L. Both obligate and facul­
tative anaerobes, including unclassified Ruminococcaceae, unclassified 
Syntrophomonadaceae, and unclassified Actinomycetaceae, were pre­
dominant during micro-aeration. The standardized performance index 
indicated Aminicenantes as the key bacteria responsible for improving 
system performance during micro-aeration. The nature of co-substrates 
and system alkalinity played an important role in the positive effects of 
micro-aeration, likely due to bicarbonate concentration, homoaceto­
genic activity, and the absence of syntrophic acetate oxidizers.
